title: Infancy Gospel of Thomas

stories.title: 📜 Infancy Gospel of Thomas
summaryBullets: At age five, Jesus plays by a stream, gathers water into pools, and commands them to obey (ch. 2).
He shapes twelve sparrows from clay and brings them to life when rebuked for working on the Sabbath (ch. 2).
Bystanders marvel, but others accuse him of breaking the law by creating on the Sabbath (ch. 2).
Another child scatters the pools; Jesus curses him, and the boy withers (ch. 3).
A boy runs into Jesus, and Jesus declares, 'You shall not finish your course,' and the child falls dead (ch. 4).
The people complain to Joseph, fearing Jesus’ power (ch. 5).
Joseph admonishes Jesus, who answers sharply, causing further fear among the townsfolk (ch. 5).
A teacher named Zacchaeus tries to teach Jesus letters, but Jesus explains the hidden meanings of Alpha and Beta (ch. 6).
The teacher marvels at his wisdom, saying no man can comprehend such mysteries (ch. 6).
Other teachers are confounded, unable to correct or control him (ch. 7).
Jesus reveals knowledge beyond human learning, silencing the elders (ch. 8).
Jesus heals a child struck down, raising him alive again (ch. 9).
He miraculously lengthens a beam of wood to help Joseph in carpentry (ch. 10).
He provides corn for the poor and heals many who come to him (ch. 11).
The people marvel, saying God is working through him, though some still fear his power (ch. 11).
At age twelve, Jesus travels with his parents to Jerusalem for the Passover (ch. 19).
He stays behind in the Temple, sitting among teachers and questioning them (ch. 19).
All marvel at his understanding and answers, recognizing divine wisdom in him (ch. 19).
Mary and Joseph find him and he replies, 'Do you not know I must be about my Father’s business?' (ch. 19).
crossRefs: Luke 2:41-52: Jesus at twelve stays behind in Jerusalem after the Passover, is found after three days among the teachers, and goes home and is subject to his parents, growing in wisdom and in favour with God and man; it is the only episode from these years the Gospels record, and this book closes on it.

John 2:11: The water made wine at Cana is called the first of his signs, by which he showed his glory and his disciples believed in him, which places the first miracle at the opening of his ministry rather than in childhood.

Luke 9:51-56: James and John ask permission to call fire down on a Samaritan village that will not receive him, and he turns and rebukes them, which is the canonical answer to power used against people who give offence.

Luke 6:27-28: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you, spoken by the same teacher this book has cursing children who knock into him in the street.

John 3:17: God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved, the stated purpose against which the witherings and the deaths in these episodes have to be read.

Exodus 20:8-11: Remember the sabbath day to keep it holy, six days you shall labour but the seventh is a sabbath to the LORD, the commandment the neighbours accuse the boy of breaking when they find him shaping clay.

Mark 2:23-28: The disciples pluck heads of grain on the sabbath, Jesus answers with what David did when he was hungry, and says the sabbath was made for man and not man for the sabbath, which is how the Gospels settle a sabbath charge.

Deuteronomy 22:8: A parapet must be built around the roof of a new house so that no one falls from it and brings bloodguilt on the household, the building law that makes a child falling from a rooftop a question of blame rather than an accident.

translationNotes.note: The earliest witnesses do not claim Thomas at all. They carry the title The Childhood Deeds of Jesus, and the first-person claim by Thomas the Israelite stands only at the head of the later Greek manuscripts. This book is also not the Gospel of Thomas, which is a collection of sayings with no story in it. The two share a name and nothing else.

In 2024 Lajos Berkes and Gabriel Nocchi Macedo recognised a papyrus scrap in the state and university library at Hamburg as a copy of this text and published the first edition of it. It measures about eleven centimetres by five, carries thirteen lines of Greek, dates to the fourth or fifth century, and preserves the opening of the clay sparrows episode. Until then the oldest Greek copy known was of the eleventh century.

The cheapest bird in the market and the poor man's meat. Matthew 10:29 prices two of them at an assarion, a copper coin worth a sixteenth of a day's wage, and Luke 12:6 prices five for two assaria, so the fifth is thrown in for nothing. That is the whole force of the saying that not one of them falls without the Father. Here the boy shapes twelve out of clay and claps his hands to send them off.

The commandment forbids melakhah, purposeful constructive work, not effort in general. Exodus 20:8-11 gives the command and Exodus 31:14-15 attaches the death penalty. The rabbinic tradition later collected in the Mishnah tractate Shabbat sorts the prohibition into thirty-nine categories, and kneading and building are two of them, which is precisely what a child working wet clay into shapes is doing.

Not the tax collector of Luke 19:1-10, who is a different man in a different town. The name is the Hebrew Zakkai, pure or innocent, and it was common. This Zacchaeus is a schoolmaster of the elementary sort who taught letters for a fee, and he asks Joseph to hand the boy over so he can be taught properly.

The alphabet in order was the first thing a Greek schoolboy learned, chanted before anything else. The boy here refuses to go on to the beta until the teacher can say what the alpha is, and then expounds the strokes of the letter itself. Irenaeus of Lyons repeats that exchange in Against Heresies 1.20.1, written about AD 180, reporting it as material the Marcosians used, which puts the episode in circulation by then.

Not a furniture maker. A tekton worked in wood and stone and put up structures: roof beams, doors, door frames, ploughs and yokes. Mark 6:3 calls Jesus the tekton and Matthew 13:55 calls him the tekton's son. The episode of the beam cut too short and pulled out to length is a builder's problem, and so is the couch that a rich man had ordered and Joseph had botched.

The measure the harvest is counted in. A kor is the same as a homer, about 220 litres of grain, and Ezekiel 45:14 fixes it at ten baths. A single sowing yielding a hundred kors is the whole point of the episode. It is the same word Luke 16:7 uses when the dishonest steward tells the debtor to write down a hundred measures of wheat.

Where the boy calls the poor of the village to take the grain. A threshing floor was a hard, flat, open patch on high ground where oxen trod out the harvest and the wind carried off the chaff when it was tossed up with a fork. It doubled as a place of public business and public mourning: Genesis 50:10 has Joseph hold a seven-day mourning for Jacob at one, and Ruth 3:6-9 has Ruth go down to Boaz at his.

A boy who breaks up the pools withers; a boy who runs into him falls dead; the neighbours who complain are struck blind. The canonical record runs the other way at every point. John 2:11 makes the water into wine the first of his signs. Luke 9:51-56 has him rebuke the disciples for wanting fire called down on a village that snubbed him. Luke 23:34 has him ask forgiveness for the men driving the nails.

The child who falls from the roof is named Zeno, and the boy is accused of pushing him. Houses had flat roofs used for sleeping, drying fruit and storage, reached by an outside stair, which is why Deuteronomy 22:8 requires a parapet around a new one so that no bloodguilt falls on the household. Mark 2:4 has four men dig through a roof of that kind to lower a paralysed man into the room below.

James is bitten on the hand while gathering sticks, and the boy blows on the bite. Acts 28:3-6 has a viper fasten on Paul's hand as he lays sticks on a fire at Malta, and the islanders watch for him to swell up or drop dead and change their verdict on him when he does not. Mark 16:18 lists taking up serpents among the signs that would follow.

Deuteronomy 16:16 requires every male to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Unleavened Bread, at Weeks and at Booths. Luke 2:41 says his parents went up every year for the Passover, and from Nazareth that is a walk of some eighty miles made in a travelling company. That is how a boy goes missing for a whole day unnoticed: everyone assumes he is somewhere else in the caravan.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου (en tois tou patros mou)
translationNotes.note: The Greek of Luke 2:49 is elliptical, literally in the things of my Father, with the noun left out. English versions fill the gap either as about my Father's business or in my Father's house, and the words carry both. This book ends on that line, which is the one saying from these years that Scripture itself records.

Three teachers take the boy in turn and are confounded. Village schooling meant one master with a small class, seated, the pupils reciting after him line by line. Luke 2:46 has the twelve-year-old in the temple sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions, which is the posture of a pupil, and Luke 2:47 says those who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.

The first episode has him gather running water into pools and make it clean at a word, and another boy scatters them with a stick. Water in the dry season came from a spring, a stream or a cistern, and holding and controlling it was work that decided whether a village ate. Genesis 26:17-22 has Isaac's herdsmen and the men of Gerar quarrel over one well after another until Isaac digs one nobody contests.

stories.keyTakeaway: Episodes from years the Gospels pass over, from Jesus at five to Jesus at twelve. Clay sparrows made to fly on the Sabbath, a boy who withers and a boy who falls dead, three teachers confounded over the alphabet, a beam pulled out to length, a viper's bite blown away, a hundred measures of grain out of one sowing, and at the end the Passover in Jerusalem that Luke records.

intro:
The Infancy Gospel of Thomas is not the Gospel of Thomas, and the two are confused constantly. The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of sayings with no story in it; this book is all story and carries almost no teaching. They share a name and nothing else.

The book covers years the Gospels pass over, from Jesus at five to Jesus at twelve. At five he is playing at a stream, gathering the running water into pools; he shapes twelve sparrows out of clay, and when he is charged with breaking the Sabbath he brings them to life. A boy scatters the pools and withers. A boy runs into him and falls dead. The neighbours complain to Joseph in fear, and Joseph rebukes him and is answered sharply. A teacher named Zacchaeus takes him through the alphabet and gets the hidden meaning of Alpha and Beta in return; two more teachers try and are confounded. He raises a child who has fallen, stretches a beam that Joseph has cut short, provides corn for the poor, and heals many who come to him. The last episode, at twelve, is the Passover in Jerusalem, Jesus left behind and found in the temple among the teachers, and his answer to his mother, which Luke records (Luke 2:41-52). The text presented here runs from chapter 2 to chapter 19.

The recensions differ widely. The best known Greek form, Greek A, has nineteen chapters and is known from manuscripts of the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. A shorter Greek form, lacking chapters 17 and 18 and standing closer to the early translations, is the form of the oldest copies; two further Greek forms prefix Egyptian episodes or abridge the whole. The earliest witnesses are not Greek at all: a Latin palimpsest at Vienna, Codex 563, of the fifth century, and a Syriac manuscript in London, British Library Additional 14484, of the sixth. Versions survive in Latin, Syriac, Georgian, Ethiopic, Church Slavonic, Irish, Armenian, and Arabic, and they do not agree on how many episodes there are or in what order they stand.

The oldest copy known was identified only recently. In 2024 Lajos Berkes and Gabriel Nocchi Macedo recognized a papyrus scrap in the Carl von Ossietzky State and University Library at Hamburg, catalogued as P.Hamb.Graec. 1011, as a copy of this text and published the first edition of it. It measures about eleven centimetres by five, carries thirteen lines of Greek, dates to the fourth or fifth century, and preserves the opening of the episode of the clay sparrows. Until then the oldest Greek copy known was of the eleventh century.

The earliest witnesses do not claim Thomas. They carry the title The Childhood Deeds of Jesus, and the first-person claim by Thomas the Israelite stands at the head of the later Greek manuscripts. The episode of the alphabet was in circulation by about AD 180: Irenaeus of Lyons, in Against Heresies 1.20.1, reports that the Marcosians used apocryphal writings and repeats the exchange in which a teacher tells the boy Jesus to say Alpha and he asks the teacher to tell him first what Alpha is. Irenaeus does not name the book he is quoting. The Gelasian Decree, transmitted under the name of Pope Gelasius I (AD 492-496) and dated in its present form to the sixth century, condemns as apocryphal the Gospel in the name of Thomas which the Manichaeans use, without saying which of the works then circulating under the name of Thomas it means. No communion receives this book as canonical.
